{"query":"link no telemetry missing data collector gap versus link down","results":[{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":8.303,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"},{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":7.389,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"}]}

{"query":"link no telemetry collector gap versus link down, traffic reroute","results":[{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":4.755,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"},{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":4.692,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"}]}

{"query":"link no telemetry after planned outage collector gap vs link down","results":[{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":5.794,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"},{"runbook":"RB08_maintenance_and_drains","score":5.159,"text":"# RB08 Planned maintenance and drains (general)

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.
- A no-op entry is logged work that did not touch traffic.
- During and just after a change window, alerts on the changed element and on links that took its traffic are expected.

How to decide:
- If every alerted element is the changed element or carries its rerouted traffic, and nothing else is abnormal, the answer is planned maintenance, not a fault.
- A fault can still happen during maintenance: look for symptoms on elements the change does not explain.
- Do not blame the changed element for symptoms that started before the change window.
"}]}

calls.output:
{"query":"link no telemetry no_data collector gap versus link down traffic reroute","results":[{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":4.755,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"},{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":4.692,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"}]}

{"query":"link no telemetry missing data versus link down, collector gap","results":[{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":8.303,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"},{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":7.389,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"}]}

{"query":"link no telemetry data blanked collector gap vs link down","results":[{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":7.917,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"},{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":5.95,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"}]}

{"query":"link no data telemetry gap versus link down or node down, distinguishing BR PoP single attached link","results":[{"runbook":"RB03_node_down","score":6.399,"text":"# RB03 Router (PoP) down

Fault type: node_down. Root: a PoP (router).

Symptoms:
- The router stops answering polls (pop_unreachable) when status polling exists.
- Every link attached to the router goes dark or reads zero at the same time.
- Services that start or end at the PoP become unreachable; services that transited it reroute.

Checks:
- Do all links of one PoP show the same outage at the same step? A single dark link is a link fault; all links of one router is the router.
- Is there a planned outage on the PoP in the change log?

Action: dispatch to the site; check power and control plane; confirm traffic has moved to alternate paths.
"},{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":5.965,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"}]}

{"query":"link saturated utilization 100% discards step change demand surge versus routing misconfig","results":[{"runbook":"RB06_demand_surge","score":4.129,"text":"# RB06 Demand surge at a PoP

Fault type: demand_surge. Root: a PoP (the source of the extra traffic).

Symptoms:
- Utilisation rises together on several links attached to one PoP, ramping up over some steps rather than jumping.
- Downstream links on paths from that PoP may hit high utilisation (link_util_high) and start to discard.
- Latency and loss rise on services from that PoP once links congest.

Checks:
- Do the busiest links share one end router? The shared router is the root, not the busiest single link.
- Is the rise larger than the normal daily pattern? Compare with the same window one day earlier.
- A drain in the change log also raises utilisation on neighbouring links; check that first.

Action: identify the traffic source; apply rate limits or add capacity; reroute where possible.
"},{"runbook":"RB07_routing_misconfig","score":3.544,"text":"# RB07 Routing misconfiguration (link metric change)

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.
"}]}

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:

"},{"runbook":"RB05_link_degradation","score":4.809,"text":"# RB05 Link degradation (loss or latency)

Fault type: link_degradation. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The link stays up, but its one-hop latency rises (link_latency_high) or it drops packets (link_discards).

{"query":"link no telemetry collector gap versus link down","results":[{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":4.524,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"},{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":4.518,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"}]}

{"query":"link no telemetry data utilization shifts to alternate path link down","results":[{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":3.439,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"},{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":2.983,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"}]}

{"query":"node down router all links no data telemetry silent","results":[{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":4.734,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"},{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":3.661,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"}]}

Fault type: node_down. Root: a PoP (router).

Symptoms:
- The router stops answering polls (pop_unreachable) when status polling exists.
- Every link attached to the router goes dark or reads zero at the same time.
- Services that start or end at the PoP become unreachable; services that transited it reroute.

Checks:
- Do all links of one PoP show the same outage at the same step? A single dark link is a link fault; all links of one router is the router.
- Is there a planned outage on the PoP in the change log?

"},{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":5.795,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.

- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.

"},{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":4.423,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.

{"query":"link_no_data all links at a PoP node down vs collector gap","results":[{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":5.795,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"},{"runbook":"RB03_node_down","score":4.713,"text":"# RB03 Router (PoP) down

Fault type: node_down. Root: a PoP (router).

Symptoms:
- The router stops answering polls (pop_unreachable) when status polling exists.
- Every link attached to the router goes dark or reads zero at the same time.
- Services that start or end at the PoP become unreachable; services that transited it reroute.

Checks:
- Do all links of one PoP show the same outage at the same step? A single dark link is a link fault; all links of one router is the router.
- Is there a planned outage on the PoP in the change log?

Action: dispatch to the site; check power and control plane; confirm traffic has moved to alternate paths.
"}]}

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.

- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

{"query":"node down router PoP telemetry missing link_no_data","results":[{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":6.304,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"},{"runbook":"RB03_node_down","score":4.131,"text":"# RB03 Router (PoP) down

Fault type: node_down. Root: a PoP (router).

Symptoms:
- The router stops answering polls (pop_unreachable) when status polling exists.
- Every link attached to the router goes dark or reads zero at the same time.
- Services that start or end at the PoP become unreachable; services that transited it reroute.

Checks:
- Do all links of one PoP show the same outage at the same step? A single dark link is a link fault; all links of one router is the router.
- Is there a planned outage on the PoP in the change log?

Action: dispatch to the site; check power and control plane; confirm traffic has moved to alternate paths.
"}]}

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:

- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.

{"query":"node_down vs link_down pop unreachable both links down","results":[{"runbook":"RB03_node_down","score":7.678,"text":"# RB03 Router (PoP) down

Fault type: node_down. Root: a PoP (router).

Symptoms:
- The router stops answering polls (pop_unreachable) when status polling exists.
- Every link attached to the router goes dark or reads zero at the same time.
- Services that start or end at the PoP become unreachable; services that transited it reroute.

Checks:
- Do all links of one PoP show the same outage at the same step? A single dark link is a link fault; all links of one router is the router.
- Is there a planned outage on the PoP in the change log?

Action: dispatch to the site; check power and control plane; confirm traffic has moved to alternate paths.
"},{"runbook":"RB06_demand_surge","score":2.977,"text":"# RB06 Demand surge at a PoP

Fault type: demand_surge. Root: a PoP (the source of the extra traffic).

Symptoms:
- Utilisation rises together on several links attached to one PoP, ramping up over some steps rather than jumping.
- Downstream links on paths from that PoP may hit high utilisation (link_util_high) and start to discard.
- Latency and loss rise on services from that PoP once links congest.

Checks:
- Do the busiest links share one end router? The shared router is the root, not the busiest single link.
- Is the rise larger than the normal daily pattern? Compare with the same window one day earlier.
- A drain in the change log also raises utilisation on neighbouring links; check that first.

Action: identify the traffic source; apply rate limits or add capacity; reroute where possible.
"}]}

{"query":"node down router all links no telemetry missing util","results":[{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":4.734,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"},{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":4.581,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"}]}

Fault type: node_down. Root: a PoP (router).

Symptoms:
- The router stops answering polls (pop_unreachable) when status polling exists.
- Every link attached to the router goes dark or reads zero at the same time.
- Services that start or end at the PoP become unreachable; services that transited it reroute.

Checks:
- Do all links of one PoP show the same outage at the same step? A single dark link is a link fault; all links of one router is the router.

"},{"runbook":"RB06_demand_surge","score":4.413,"text":"# RB06 Demand surge at a PoP

Fault type: demand_surge. Root: a PoP (the source of the extra traffic).

Symptoms:
- Utilisation rises together on several links attached to one PoP, ramping up over some steps rather than jumping.
- Downstream links on paths from that PoP may hit high utilisation (link_util_high) and start to discard.
- Latency and loss rise on services from that PoP once links congest.

Checks:
- Do the busiest links share one end router? The shared router is the root, not the busiest single link.
- Is the rise larger than the normal daily pattern? Compare with the same window one day earlier.
- A drain in the change log also raises utilisation on neighbouring links; check that first.

Action: identify the traffic source; apply rate limits or add capacity; reroute where possible.
"}]}

Fault type: demand_surge. Root: a PoP (the source of the extra traffic).

Symptoms:
- Utilisation rises together on several links attached to one PoP, ramping up over some steps rather than jumping.
- Downstream links on paths from that PoP may hit high utilisation (link_util_high) and start to discard.
- Latency and loss rise on services from that PoP once links congest.

Checks:
- Do the busiest links share one end router? The shared router is the root, not the busiest single link.
- Is the rise larger than the normal daily pattern? Compare with the same window one day earlier.
- A drain in the change log also raises utilisation on neighbouring links; check that first.

Action: identify the traffic source; apply rate limits or add capacity; reroute where possible.

Fault type: node_down. Root: a PoP (router).

Symptoms:
- The router stops answering polls (pop_unreachable) when status polling exists.
- Every link attached to the router goes dark or reads zero at the same time.
- Services that start or end at the PoP become unreachable; services that transited it reroute.

Checks:
- Do all links of one PoP show the same outage at the same step? A single dark link is a link fault; all links of one router is the router.
- Is there a planned outage on the PoP in the change log?

Action: dispatch to the site; check power and control plane; confirm traffic has moved to alternate paths.
"},{"runbook":"RB06_demand_surge","score":3.463,"text":"# RB06 Demand surge at a PoP

Fault type: demand_surge. Root: a PoP (the source of the extra traffic).

Symptoms:
- Utilisation rises together on several links attached to one PoP, ramping up over some steps rather than jumping.
- Downstream links on paths from that PoP may hit high utilisation (link_util_high) and start to discard.
- Latency and loss rise on services from that PoP once links congest.

Checks:
- Do the busiest links share one end router? The shared router is the root, not the busiest single link.
- Is the rise larger than the normal daily pattern? Compare with the same window one day earlier.
- A drain in the change log also raises utilisation on neighbouring links; check that first.

Action: identify the traffic source; apply rate limits or add capacity; reroute where possible.
"}]}

- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.

calls.output:
{"query":"link_no_data alert collector gap blanked telemetry link down","results":[{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":6.383,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"},{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":5.76,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"}]}

Fault type: node_down. Root: a PoP (router).

Symptoms:
- The router stops answering polls (pop_unreachable) when status polling exists.

- Services that start or end at the PoP become unreachable; services that transited it reroute.

Checks:

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.

"},{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":4.95,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.

Fault type: link_flapping. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface goes down and up repeatedly; several short link_status_down alerts on the same link, or intermittent gaps in its telemetry.
- Repeated short bursts of loss on services that cross the link as routing converges each time.

Fault type: link_degradation. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The link stays up, but its one-hop latency rises (link_latency_high) or it drops packets (link_discards).

- Utilisation is often unchanged, because routing does not move traffic away from a degraded but up link.

- Compare the link's latency and discards with the same window one day earlier.
- Find the element shared by the paths of the services with SLA alerts; a degraded link is usually on all of them.
- Small degradations may raise no alert: look at the telemetry of links on the shared paths even without alerts.

Action: raise with the transmission team; consider moving traffic off the link with a metric change.

Fault type: link_flapping. Root: a link.

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.

- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Fault type: link_flapping. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface goes down and up repeatedly; several short link_status_down alerts on the same link, or intermittent gaps in its telemetry.
- Repeated short bursts of loss on services that cross the link as routing converges each time.
- Utilisation on the link drops and recovers repeatedly; neighbours show matching opposite swings.

Checks:
- Count down/up episodes on the link in the window: more than one short episode is the signature.
- Rule out a collector problem: intermittent gaps on many unrelated links at once are not flapping.

Action: dampen or shut the interface and reroute; check optics and physical layer.
"},{"runbook":"RB05_link_degradation","score":4.245,"text":"# RB05 Link degradation (loss or latency)

Fault type: link_degradation. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The link stays up, but its one-hop latency rises (link_latency_high) or it drops packets (link_discards).
- Services crossing the link breach latency or loss SLAs; services not crossing it are fine.
- Utilisation is often unchanged, because routing does not move traffic away from a degraded but up link.

Checks:
- Compare the link's latency and discards with the same window one day earlier.
- Find the element shared by the paths of the services with SLA alerts; a degraded link is usually on all of them.
- Small degradations may raise no alert: look at the telemetry of links on the shared paths even without alerts.

Action: raise with the transmission team; consider moving traffic off the link with a metric change.

{"query":"high discards with low utilization link degradation","results":[{"runbook":"RB05_link_degradation","score":3.953,"text":"# RB05 Link degradation (loss or latency)

Fault type: link_degradation. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The link stays up, but its one-hop latency rises (link_latency_high) or it drops packets (link_discards).
- Services crossing the link breach latency or loss SLAs; services not crossing it are fine.
- Utilisation is often unchanged, because routing does not move traffic away from a degraded but up link.

Checks:
- Compare the link's latency and discards with the same window one day earlier.
- Find the element shared by the paths of the services with SLA alerts; a degraded link is usually on all of them.
- Small degradations may raise no alert: look at the telemetry of links on the shared paths even without alerts.

Action: raise with the transmission team; consider moving traffic off the link with a metric change.
"},{"runbook":"RB06_demand_surge","score":1.946,"text":"# RB06 Demand surge at a PoP

Fault type: demand_surge. Root: a PoP (the source of the extra traffic).

Symptoms:
- Utilisation rises together on several links attached to one PoP, ramping up over some steps rather than jumping.
- Downstream links on paths from that PoP may hit high utilisation (link_util_high) and start to discard.
- Latency and loss rise on services from that PoP once links congest.

Checks:
- Do the busiest links share one end router? The shared router is the root, not the busiest single link.
- Is the rise larger than the normal daily pattern? Compare with the same window one day earlier.
- A drain in the change log also raises utilisation on neighbouring links; check that first.

Action: identify the traffic source; apply rate limits or add capacity; reroute where possible.
"}]}

{"query":"link discards degradation flapping versus down distinguish","results":[{"runbook":"RB05_link_degradation","score":3.953,"text":"# RB05 Link degradation (loss or latency)

Fault type: link_degradation. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The link stays up, but its one-hop latency rises (link_latency_high) or it drops packets (link_discards).
- Services crossing the link breach latency or loss SLAs; services not crossing it are fine.
- Utilisation is often unchanged, because routing does not move traffic away from a degraded but up link.

Checks:
- Compare the link's latency and discards with the same window one day earlier.
- Find the element shared by the paths of the services with SLA alerts; a degraded link is usually on all of them.
- Small degradations may raise no alert: look at the telemetry of links on the shared paths even without alerts.

Action: raise with the transmission team; consider moving traffic off the link with a metric change.
"},{"runbook":"RB04_link_flapping","score":3.644,"text":"# RB04 Link flapping

Fault type: link_flapping. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface goes down and up repeatedly; several short link_status_down alerts on the same link, or intermittent gaps in its telemetry.
- Repeated short bursts of loss on services that cross the link as routing converges each time.
- Utilisation on the link drops and recovers repeatedly; neighbours show matching opposite swings.

Checks:
- Count down/up episodes on the link in the window: more than one short episode is the signature.
- Rule out a collector problem: intermittent gaps on many unrelated links at once are not flapping.

Action: dampen or shut the interface and reroute; check optics and physical layer.
"}]}

{"query":"link discards degradation vs flapping interface errors","results":[{"runbook":"RB04_link_flapping","score":4.586,"text":"# RB04 Link flapping

Fault type: link_flapping. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface goes down and up repeatedly; several short link_status_down alerts on the same link, or intermittent gaps in its telemetry.
- Repeated short bursts of loss on services that cross the link as routing converges each time.
- Utilisation on the link drops and recovers repeatedly; neighbours show matching opposite swings.

Checks:
- Count down/up episodes on the link in the window: more than one short episode is the signature.
- Rule out a collector problem: intermittent gaps on many unrelated links at once are not flapping.

Action: dampen or shut the interface and reroute; check optics and physical layer.
"},{"runbook":"RB05_link_degradation","score":3.953,"text":"# RB05 Link degradation (loss or latency)

Fault type: link_degradation. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The link stays up, but its one-hop latency rises (link_latency_high) or it drops packets (link_discards).
- Services crossing the link breach latency or loss SLAs; services not crossing it are fine.
- Utilisation is often unchanged, because routing does not move traffic away from a degraded but up link.

Checks:
- Compare the link's latency and discards with the same window one day earlier.
- Find the element shared by the paths of the services with SLA alerts; a degraded link is usually on all of them.
- Small degradations may raise no alert: look at the telemetry of links on the shared paths even without alerts.

Action: raise with the transmission team; consider moving traffic off the link with a metric change.
"}]}

{"query":"routing metric change traffic shift link utilization drop without change log","results":[{"runbook":"RB07_routing_misconfig","score":4.914,"text":"# RB07 Routing misconfiguration (link metric change)

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.
"},{"runbook":"RB05_link_degradation","score":4.518,"text":"# RB05 Link degradation (loss or latency)

Fault type: link_degradation. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The link stays up, but its one-hop latency rises (link_latency_high) or it drops packets (link_discards).
- Services crossing the link breach latency or loss SLAs; services not crossing it are fine.
- Utilisation is often unchanged, because routing does not move traffic away from a degraded but up link.

Checks:
- Compare the link's latency and discards with the same window one day earlier.
- Find the element shared by the paths of the services with SLA alerts; a degraded link is usually on all of them.
- Small degradations may raise no alert: look at the telemetry of links on the shared paths even without alerts.

Action: raise with the transmission team; consider moving traffic off the link with a metric change.
"}]}

Fault type: link_flapping. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface goes down and up repeatedly; several short link_status_down alerts on the same link, or intermittent gaps in its telemetry.
- Repeated short bursts of loss on services that cross the link as routing converges each time.
- Utilisation on the link drops and recovers repeatedly; neighbours show matching opposite swings.

- Rule out a collector problem: intermittent gaps on many unrelated links at once are not flapping.

"},{"runbook":"RB05_link_degradation","score":3.953,"text":"# RB05 Link degradation (loss or latency)

Fault type: link_degradation. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The link stays up, but its one-hop latency rises (link_latency_high) or it drops packets (link_discards).
- Services crossing the link breach latency or loss SLAs; services not crossing it are fine.
- Utilisation is often unchanged, because routing does not move traffic away from a degraded but up link.

Checks:
- Compare the link's latency and discards with the same window one day earlier.
- Find the element shared by the paths of the services with SLA alerts; a degraded link is usually on all of them.
- Small degradations may raise no alert: look at the telemetry of links on the shared paths even without alerts.

Action: raise with the transmission team; consider moving traffic off the link with a metric change.

- The link stays up, but its one-hop latency rises (link_latency_high) or it drops packets (link_discards).

- Find the element shared by the paths of the services with SLA alerts; a degraded link is usually on all of them.

{"query":"planned outage link down probe unreachable services after maintenance","results":[{"runbook":"RB08_maintenance_and_drains","score":5.952,"text":"# RB08 Planned maintenance and drains (general)

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.
- A no-op entry is logged work that did not touch traffic.
- During and just after a change window, alerts on the changed element and on links that took its traffic are expected.

How to decide:
- If every alerted element is the changed element or carries its rerouted traffic, and nothing else is abnormal, the answer is planned maintenance, not a fault.
- A fault can still happen during maintenance: look for symptoms on elements the change does not explain.
- Do not blame the changed element for symptoms that started before the change window.
"},{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":4.863,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.

{"query":"planned outage maintenance link probe fail after restore","results":[{"runbook":"RB08_maintenance_and_drains","score":5.215,"text":"# RB08 Planned maintenance and drains (general)

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.
- A no-op entry is logged work that did not touch traffic.
- During and just after a change window, alerts on the changed element and on links that took its traffic are expected.

How to decide:
- If every alerted element is the changed element or carries its rerouted traffic, and nothing else is abnormal, the answer is planned maintenance, not a fault.
- A fault can still happen during maintenance: look for symptoms on elements the change does not explain.
- Do not blame the changed element for symptoms that started before the change window.
"},{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":3.894,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"}]}

{"query":"traffic shift utilisation rise on adjacent links, link down, reroute","results":[{"runbook":"RB06_demand_surge","score":4.102,"text":"# RB06 Demand surge at a PoP

Fault type: demand_surge. Root: a PoP (the source of the extra traffic).

Symptoms:
- Utilisation rises together on several links attached to one PoP, ramping up over some steps rather than jumping.
- Downstream links on paths from that PoP may hit high utilisation (link_util_high) and start to discard.
- Latency and loss rise on services from that PoP once links congest.

Checks:
- Do the busiest links share one end router? The shared router is the root, not the busiest single link.
- Is the rise larger than the normal daily pattern? Compare with the same window one day earlier.
- A drain in the change log also raises utilisation on neighbouring links; check that first.

Action: identify the traffic source; apply rate limits or add capacity; reroute where possible.
"},{"runbook":"RB08_maintenance_and_drains","score":2.666,"text":"# RB08 Planned maintenance and drains (general)

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.
- A no-op entry is logged work that did not touch traffic.
- During and just after a change window, alerts on the changed element and on links that took its traffic are expected.

How to decide:
- If every alerted element is the changed element or carries its rerouted traffic, and nothing else is abnormal, the answer is planned maintenance, not a fault.
- A fault can still happen during maintenance: look for symptoms on elements the change does not explain.
- Do not blame the changed element for symptoms that started before the change window.
"}]}

{"query":"link saturation high utilisation discards latency rise diagnosis demand surge vs capacity degradation vs routing metric","results":[{"runbook":"RB06_demand_surge","score":10.01,"text":"# RB06 Demand surge at a PoP

Fault type: demand_surge. Root: a PoP (the source of the extra traffic).

Symptoms:
- Utilisation rises together on several links attached to one PoP, ramping up over some steps rather than jumping.
- Downstream links on paths from that PoP may hit high utilisation (link_util_high) and start to discard.
- Latency and loss rise on services from that PoP once links congest.

Checks:
- Do the busiest links share one end router? The shared router is the root, not the busiest single link.
- Is the rise larger than the normal daily pattern? Compare with the same window one day earlier.
- A drain in the change log also raises utilisation on neighbouring links; check that first.

Action: identify the traffic source; apply rate limits or add capacity; reroute where possible.
"},{"runbook":"RB05_link_degradation","score":6.702,"text":"# RB05 Link degradation (loss or latency)

Fault type: link_degradation. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The link stays up, but its one-hop latency rises (link_latency_high) or it drops packets (link_discards).
- Services crossing the link breach latency or loss SLAs; services not crossing it are fine.
- Utilisation is often unchanged, because routing does not move traffic away from a degraded but up link.

Checks:
- Compare the link's latency and discards with the same window one day earlier.
- Find the element shared by the paths of the services with SLA alerts; a degraded link is usually on all of them.
- Small degradations may raise no alert: look at the telemetry of links on the shared paths even without alerts.

Action: raise with the transmission team; consider moving traffic off the link with a metric change.
"}]}

{"query":"planned traffic drain routing metric restore after maintenance window","results":[{"runbook":"RB08_maintenance_and_drains","score":7.923,"text":"# RB08 Planned maintenance and drains (general)

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.
- A no-op entry is logged work that did not touch traffic.
- During and just after a change window, alerts on the changed element and on links that took its traffic are expected.

How to decide:
- If every alerted element is the changed element or carries its rerouted traffic, and nothing else is abnormal, the answer is planned maintenance, not a fault.
- A fault can still happen during maintenance: look for symptoms on elements the change does not explain.
- Do not blame the changed element for symptoms that started before the change window.
"},{"runbook":"RB07_routing_misconfig","score":3.879,"text":"# RB07 Routing misconfiguration (link metric change)

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.
"}]}

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.

"},{"runbook":"RB06_demand_surge","score":2.466,"text":"# RB06 Demand surge at a PoP

Fault type: demand_surge. Root: a PoP (the source of the extra traffic).

- Utilisation rises together on several links attached to one PoP, ramping up over some steps rather than jumping.

- Latency and loss rise on services from that PoP once links congest.

Checks:
- Do the busiest links share one end router? The shared router is the root, not the busiest single link.
- Is the rise larger than the normal daily pattern? Compare with the same window one day earlier.
- A drain in the change log also raises utilisation on neighbouring links; check that first.

{"query":"traffic shifted to parallel link, routing metric change, saturated link discards","results":[{"runbook":"RB05_link_degradation","score":4.335,"text":"# RB05 Link degradation (loss or latency)

Fault type: link_degradation. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The link stays up, but its one-hop latency rises (link_latency_high) or it drops packets (link_discards).
- Services crossing the link breach latency or loss SLAs; services not crossing it are fine.
- Utilisation is often unchanged, because routing does not move traffic away from a degraded but up link.

Checks:
- Compare the link's latency and discards with the same window one day earlier.
- Find the element shared by the paths of the services with SLA alerts; a degraded link is usually on all of them.
- Small degradations may raise no alert: look at the telemetry of links on the shared paths even without alerts.

Action: raise with the transmission team; consider moving traffic off the link with a metric change.
"},{"runbook":"RB07_routing_misconfig","score":4.064,"text":"# RB07 Routing misconfiguration (link metric change)

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.

"},{"runbook":"RB08_maintenance_and_drains","score":5.897,"text":"# RB08 Planned maintenance and drains (general)

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.
- A no-op entry is logged work that did not touch traffic.
- During and just after a change window, alerts on the changed element and on links that took its traffic are expected.

How to decide:
- If every alerted element is the changed element or carries its rerouted traffic, and nothing else is abnormal, the answer is planned maintenance, not a fault.
- A fault can still happen during maintenance: look for symptoms on elements the change does not explain.
- Do not blame the changed element for symptoms that started before the change window.
"}]}

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.

"},{"runbook":"RB05_link_degradation","score":4.518,"text":"# RB05 Link degradation (loss or latency)

Fault type: link_degradation. Root: a link.

- Utilisation is often unchanged, because routing does not move traffic away from a degraded but up link.

{"query":"routing metric change traffic shift link utilization drop link still up","results":[{"runbook":"RB07_routing_misconfig","score":4.637,"text":"# RB07 Routing misconfiguration (link metric change)

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.
"},{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":3.82,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.

Fault type: link_degradation. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The link stays up, but its one-hop latency rises (link_latency_high) or it drops packets (link_discards).
- Services crossing the link breach latency or loss SLAs; services not crossing it are fine.
- Utilisation is often unchanged, because routing does not move traffic away from a degraded but up link.

Checks:
- Compare the link's latency and discards with the same window one day earlier.
- Find the element shared by the paths of the services with SLA alerts; a degraded link is usually on all of them.

Action: raise with the transmission team; consider moving traffic off the link with a metric change.
"},{"runbook":"RB07_routing_misconfig","score":5.791,"text":"# RB07 Routing misconfiguration (link metric change)

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.

"},{"runbook":"RB05_link_degradation","score":6.257,"text":"# RB05 Link degradation (loss or latency)

Fault type: link_degradation. Root: a link.

- Utilisation is often unchanged, because routing does not move traffic away from a degraded but up link.

- Compare the link's latency and discards with the same window one day earlier.

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.
"},{"runbook":"RB08_maintenance_and_drains","score":4.582,"text":"# RB08 Planned maintenance and drains (general)

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.
- A no-op entry is logged work that did not touch traffic.
- During and just after a change window, alerts on the changed element and on links that took its traffic are expected.

How to decide:
- If every alerted element is the changed element or carries its rerouted traffic, and nothing else is abnormal, the answer is planned maintenance, not a fault.
- A fault can still happen during maintenance: look for symptoms on elements the change does not explain.
- Do not blame the changed element for symptoms that started before the change window.
"}]}

- Compare the link's latency and discards with the same window one day earlier.

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.

"},{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":5.113,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.

{"query":"pop unreachable node down versus collector gap no data","results":[{"runbook":"RB03_node_down","score":5.335,"text":"# RB03 Router (PoP) down

Fault type: node_down. Root: a PoP (router).

Symptoms:
- The router stops answering polls (pop_unreachable) when status polling exists.
- Every link attached to the router goes dark or reads zero at the same time.
- Services that start or end at the PoP become unreachable; services that transited it reroute.

Checks:
- Do all links of one PoP show the same outage at the same step? A single dark link is a link fault; all links of one router is the router.
- Is there a planned outage on the PoP in the change log?

Action: dispatch to the site; check power and control plane; confirm traffic has moved to alternate paths.
"},{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":5.298,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"}]}

{"query":"link_no_data telemetry gap versus node down unreachable services","results":[{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":4.991,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"},{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":2.846,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"}]}

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.
- A no-op entry is logged work that did not touch traffic.
- During and just after a change window, alerts on the changed element and on links that took its traffic are expected.

How to decide:
- If every alerted element is the changed element or carries its rerouted traffic, and nothing else is abnormal, the answer is planned maintenance, not a fault.
- A fault can still happen during maintenance: look for symptoms on elements the change does not explain.
- Do not blame the changed element for symptoms that started before the change window.
"},{"runbook":"RB06_demand_surge","score":3.408,"text":"# RB06 Demand surge at a PoP

Fault type: demand_surge. Root: a PoP (the source of the extra traffic).

Symptoms:
- Utilisation rises together on several links attached to one PoP, ramping up over some steps rather than jumping.
- Downstream links on paths from that PoP may hit high utilisation (link_util_high) and start to discard.
- Latency and loss rise on services from that PoP once links congest.

Checks:
- Do the busiest links share one end router? The shared router is the root, not the busiest single link.
- Is the rise larger than the normal daily pattern? Compare with the same window one day earlier.
- A drain in the change log also raises utilisation on neighbouring links; check that first.

Action: identify the traffic source; apply rate limits or add capacity; reroute where possible.
